messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 38

He is a 33-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life helping other people move through pain. As a physical therapist, he is used to noticing small shifts in posture, the way a person guards an injured shoulder, the hesitation before weight is put onto a healing leg. He speaks calmly with patients, and he is known for being patient and steady, even when progress is slow. Friends and coworkers describe him as dependable. He has built a life around competence, care, and control, and before the accident, those qualities seemed to carry him through almost everything.

The accident happens on an ordinary afternoon and shatters that sense of predictability. He is driving home after work when another vehicle crosses into his lane at high speed. In the split second before impact, he sees the other car coming and has time only for a brief, frozen awareness that he cannot avoid it. The collision is violent. Metal crumples, glass bursts, and the world turns into sound and force. He remembers the smell of gasoline, the sting of airbags, and the terrifying sense that he cannot tell where his body ends and the wreck begins. For a few moments he is certain he is dying. Later, he will say that what frightened him most was not the pain, but the helplessness of being trapped while his mind kept insisting this could not be happening.

In the days after the accident, he moves through the medical workup in a fog. Physically, he is bruised and sore, but the emotional shock is harder to describe. He sleeps poorly and wakes repeatedly with his heart racing, as if something is still approaching him. At night, when he closes his eyes, he sees the instant before the crash and feels his whole body tense as though he is bracing for impact again. He startsle[s] at sudden noises, especially tires screeching or horns outside his home. His wife notices that he becomes quiet when traffic is mentioned. He says he is fine, but he is not present in the same way he was before. He checks mirrors more often while riding in a car, scans intersections with unusual intensity, and prefers to avoid driving altogether if he can help it.

Returning to work is more difficult than he expects. His profession requires him to guide others through recovery, but now he feels uncertain in his own body. He can demonstrate exercises and explain anatomy with his usual clarity, yet he finds himself distracted by images of twisted metal or by a sudden, involuntary flash of the crash scene when a car backfires outside the clinic. He becomes hyperaware of environmental sounds. If a patient arrives late after being in an accident, he feels a tightness in his chest and has to concentrate harder to stay composed. He worries that he is failing at his job because his attention drifts, but he says little about it. He is embarrassed by how much the accident lingers in him, especially because he has always seen himself as resilient.

He avoids reminders whenever possible. He takes longer routes to work to stay off the road where the crash happened. He no longer likes sitting near intersections or watching action scenes that involve collisions. Friends invite him on weekend drives or outings out of town, and he often declines without offering an explanation. Even small reminders can stir discomfort: the metallic smell of a repair shop, the sudden braking of traffic, the sight of a crushed vehicle on the highway. When this happens, his body responds before his mind can catch up. His jaw tightens, his pulse climbs, and he feels a rush of fear that is out of proportion to the moment, though it feels entirely justified to him.

At home, his wife sees the changes most clearly. He is loving, but more strained, and he is less able to relax in the evenings. He sits near the door in restaurants or public places. He becomes irritated when plans change unexpectedly. Some days he seems to be replaying the event internally, answering questions with short phrases and then going distant, as though he has left the room while his body remains. Other times, he is flooded by guilt for surviving the crash when another driver was seriously injured. He does not speak much about this guilt, but it sits beneath his silence and colors the way he talks about the future.

Still, he keeps going. He shows up to work, cares for his patients, and tries to be the husband he believes his wife deserves. But there is a visible effort in the way he does ordinary things now, as if each day requires him to push through an unseen resistance. He is not the same man who drove home that afternoon. He is living with a nervous system that no longer trusts the world to stay intact, and even as time passes, part of him remains braced for the sound of impact.
